title: Three Requisitions, Three Bands
description: The same job in the same city is advertised three times, and he applied to the cheapest. The middle advert pays ninety-five thousand more, and his own pack told him to skip it. One question, asked early, that puts the money back on the table.

lines.text: Three adverts. One company, one city, one job. He applied to the cheapest of the three.
The advert he was told to skip pays up to two hundred and seventy-five thousand dollars.
Told to skip it by whom?
By his own application pack, which said the senior version wanted leadership he could not evidence.
That was written before his evidence file gained React, full stack, and an AWS migration he led.
Then he applied to the wrong advert. That is a mistake, not a strategy.
It is a mistake, and one question on Thursday can still undo it. That is this episode.
This is The DeployCo Screen. This episode is the few minutes where money comes up.
The standard advice says never discuss salary in a first call. Deflect, and deal with it later.
That advice assumes one band you cannot see. Here there are three bands, and all three are published.
When the numbers are public there is nothing to protect. Deflecting only leaves the default in place.
The default is the advert he applied through, and it tops out exactly at his floor.
So the goal is to name a bigger number than the recruiter expects.
No. The goal is to change which advert the conversation is about, before any number is spoken.
A number argued inside the wrong requisition goes nowhere. She cannot pay above a band she does not own.
Three things about how this works inside a company.
First, a recruiter cannot exceed a band. She can move you between requisitions. She cannot rewrite one.
Surely she moves him herself if he is obviously senior. That is her job.
Sometimes. More often an application sits against the requisition it arrived on, because nobody questioned it.
His arrived on the cheapest of the three, on the eleventh of August. Nobody has questioned it yet.
Second, the first number spoken becomes the reference point for every conversation after it.
Say a hundred and seventy-five, and every later call argues about how far above that he can reach.
Let her say one thirty-five to three sixty, and the conversation starts somewhere else entirely.
Third, equity here is not an ordinary grant, because this is not an ordinary company.
DeployCo is a joint venture inside a reported ten billion dollar vehicle with nineteen investors.
Equity in a private subsidiary is a lottery ticket. Not worth spending call minutes on.
It may be. Asking what instrument it is tells you whether they know, and that is information.
Now the moment, played out. Three branches, and all three are fine if taken deliberately.
She will describe the role somewhere in the first fifteen minutes. That is the opening.
You say: can I ask which requisition this is against, because I think there may be three.
Then the reason. I applied through the Tomoro advert, which publishes one thirty to one eighty.
The same board carries a senior version of that role at one eighty to two seventy-five.
And your own board has a Sydney forward deployed engineer role at one thirty-five to three sixty.
Which am I being considered for? Four sentences, and every one checkable on her own systems.
That is a lot of homework to recite at someone. It sounds like an accusation.
Only if the tone is. Asked plainly, it reads as someone who did the reading.
Branch one. She says the forward deployed role, one thirty-five to three sixty plus equity.
Based on the scope in that advert, owning architecture across engagements, setting evaluation, mentoring.
I'd be looking at two hundred to two forty base, and I'd want to understand the equity first.
Branch two. She says the senior Tomoro requisition, one eighty to two seventy-five.
That band starts at his floor, so there is nothing to defend. He anchors at two hundred and thirty.
Two thirty on four months of production experience is greedy. She will laugh.
Two thirty sits just above the middle of a band the company published for this exact title.
He is not inventing a number. He is asking for the upper middle of their own advert.
Branch three. She says the original Tomoro requisition, one thirty to one eighty.
Do not negotiate inside that band. One eighty is his floor, so it only works at the ceiling.
Instead: I'd rather be considered against the senior version, or the forward deployed role. Can we do that?
And if she says no to both?
Then he learned it on day one instead of week four, and he lost nothing by asking.
The numbers, said twice, because they have to arrive without thinking.
One thirty to one eighty. The Tomoro advert he applied through, published September twenty twenty-five.
One eighty to two seventy-five. The senior version, same board, same publication date.
One thirty-five to three sixty plus equity. The DeployCo Sydney advert, published the seventh of August.
Again. One thirty to one eighty. One eighty to two seventy-five. One thirty-five to three sixty.
The gap between the ceiling he applied to and the senior ceiling is ninety-five thousand dollars.
Two adverts on one board, same date, ninety-five thousand apart. That sounds like an error.
It is not. It is an ordinary level split. The error was assuming he belonged in the lower one.
His floor is one hundred and eighty thousand. That number stays private and never gets said aloud.
A floor spoken aloud stops being a floor and becomes the offer.
Two hundred to two forty on the forward deployed role. Two hundred and thirty on the senior one.
The whole move in one pass, nothing new.
She describes the role. You ask which of three requisitions, and give the three bands as the reason.
Forward deployed, you tie two hundred to two forty to the scope, then ask about the equity.
Senior Tomoro, you anchor at two hundred and thirty, because that band starts at your floor.
Original Tomoro, you do not negotiate. You ask to be moved to one of the other two.
Either way, no number left your mouth before you knew which band it was landing in.
Four ways this goes wrong, each with a signal you can hear while it happens.
First, answering the expectations question directly. She asks, you answer, and it is over in four seconds.
The signal is the shape of her question. What are you looking for, salary-wise, is a request for an anchor.
Refusing a direct question is rude. Recruiters remember that.
He is not refusing. He asks one question first, then answers fully. That is not the same thing.
Second, ruling himself out of the senior band before she does. That is the new failure this week.
The signal is hearing yourself explain why you are probably not senior enough. Stop that sentence.
Let her decide the level. His job is to get all three requisitions onto the table.
Third, quoting a number but sounding unsure. Two thirty, said as a question, becomes two hundred.
The signal is your own voice rising at the end. Say the number flat, and then stop.
Fourth, negotiating against yourself in the silence. She pauses, and you fill it by coming down.
The signal is the silence itself. Recruiters use silence, and it is not disapproval.
After you name a number, the next person to speak should be her.
Three things, as questions to ask yourself during the call.
Have I asked which of the three requisitions, before any number left my mouth?
Am I letting her decide whether I am senior, instead of deciding it against myself?
Have I asked what the equity actually is, given this is a joint venture and not a normal subsidiary?
And if the call ends without money coming up at all?
Then raise the requisition question anyway, at the end, under what happens next.
Self-test. What is the first thing you say when she asks about salary expectations?
Not a number. A question about which requisition, with the three bands as the reason for asking.
Next time: the questions you ask her, and how to read the answers she gives.
